newsitem.title: USA: High USDA corn, soy data confirms end of rally.
newsitem.headline: High USDA corn, soy data confirms end of rally.

text.p: Bearish U.S. Agriculture Department corn and soybean production estimates confirmed the end of a year-long rally in Chicago Board of Trade futures and prices could fall further if USDA raises projections again in November, analysts said.

"There's quite a historical precedent for both the corn and the soy numbers to increase," said Joel Karlin, grain analyst at Everen Securities. "It seems to me the whole bull run in the soybean complex has come to a screeching halt."
USDA on Friday raised its U.S. corn production estimate to 9.012 billion bushels and soybean output to 2.346 billion.

The figures had been upwardly revised from USDA's September outlook for 8.804 billion bushels of corn and 2.270 billion bushels of soybeans. Analysts had been looking for a corn number of 8.951 billion and a soybean figure of 2.287 billion.
Merrill Lynch oilseeds analyst, Mario Balletto, said USDA could increase its November soybean production figure but would likely add fewer than 50 million bushels.
While another increase would weigh on prices, he noted that November soybean futures had already fallen $1.00 per bushel since July.

"The market is reacting very bearishly to these numbers on top of having already declined substantially prior to this report on expectations of increased supply," Balletto said. "Unless the crop gets a lot bigger from where it is right now, we may be close to putting in some lows here."
But Everen's Karlin said USDA had underestimated corn and soybean output from the eastern Corn Belt where late planting put the crop at risk of an early or even normal frost.
No freezing temperatures were forecast for the southern parts of Ohio and Indiana through next week, which lessened concerns of frost damage, he said.
"I think it's certainly within the realm of possibility that we could get a corn crop of 9.2 billion (bushels) and a bean crop of 2.4 billion," Karlin said.
December corn futures could fall to $2.60 per bushel and November soybean prices to $6.75 if USDA increased its crop projections next month, he added.
At midday Friday, December corn on the CBOT was at $2.84-1/4 a bushel and November soybeans at $7.00-1/4.
Merrill Lynch grain analyst Randy Mittelstaedt agreed USDA traditionally raises its November estimate after an increase in the October figures but said crop conditions did not favor a large hike.
"Historically, if they raise (estimates) this time they have a tendency to raise it again," Mittelstaedt said. "I think it's tough to go much above where we're at right now."
Mittelstaedt forecast corn prices holding in a $2.80 to $3.00 per bushel trading range due to low corn stocks.
"Overall we still have a tight balance sheet," he said. "You did loosen it up a little bit today but it's still historically fairly tight."
USDA put ending corn stocks at 903 million bushels, up from its previous forecast for 668 million and soybean stocks at 195 million bushels, up from the earlier forecast for 160 million.
